title: The Paper You Can't Prove Anything About
author: Winkel, Doan
source: How to Teach With AI (howtoteachwithai.substack.com), September 14, 2026
summary: This piece rejects both common responses to suspected AI-written student work — running it through a detector (an unexplainable percentage from an uninspectable black box) or confronting the student directly (a conversation that damages the relationship whether or not anything happened) — as fundamentally broken. Its proposed alternative is a universal, low-stakes three-minute oral checkpoint applied to every student on every major assignment, not just the ones a teacher suspects: three questions generated from that specific student's own submission, targeting the choices only the actual author could explain, answered aloud with the paper closed. The author is careful about implementation details that determine whether the technique feels fair: it must be announced on the syllabus before the first submission (introduced after the fact, it becomes an accusation), kept to low stakes like 10% of the grade, and evaluated on whether decisions exist behind the paper rather than on delivery or nervousness. Its most striking claim is that the checkpoint's real value isn't catching cheating at all — most of the time, it reveals that a student who wrote a mediocre paper actually understands the material far better than the page shows, information grading alone never surfaces.
points: Rejects both standard responses to suspected AI cheating — AI detectors (unexplainable black-box percentages) and direct confrontation (damages the relationship regardless of guilt) — as broken by design.
Proposes a universal 3-minute oral checkpoint for every student on every major assignment, with questions generated from each student's own specific choices, not generic prompts.
Implementation matters as much as the idea: must be a syllabus policy announced before the first submission, or it functions as an accusation with a policy taped on.
The real payoff isn't cheating detection — it's discovering that students who wrote mediocre papers often understand the material far better than their grade suggests.
quotes: The first is a detector. You paste the paper in, get a percentage, and now you're holding a number you cannot explain, produced by a system you cannot inspect, and you are supposed to stake a student's record on it.
So change what every paper comes with. Every major assignment gets a three-minute oral checkpoint. Every student, no exceptions, scheduled before anybody hands anything in.
Run on everyone, it is a course policy. Run on one person, it is a trial.
Put it on the syllabus and the assignment sheet before the first submission. A checkpoint introduced after the fact is an accusation with a policy taped to it.

The quiet win is that most of this never gets used on cheating. You will spend most of those three minutes finding out that a student who wrote a mediocre paper understands far more than they got on the page. Grading has never told you that.
